idiom_name: scala.Dynamic (selectDynamic/updateDynamic) over a mutable.Map; Selectable structural types in Scala 3
implementation_notes: Extending scala.Dynamic makes the compiler rewrite selections that do not otherwise typecheck: foo.field becomes foo.selectDynamic("field") and foo.varia = 10 becomes foo.updateDynamic("varia")(10), so a mutable.Map[String, Any] behind those two methods is the property list and the class is the owner. Dynamic member selection is feature-gated because it can undermine static checkability of programs, which is also why Scala 3's Selectable with structural types is the checked sibling for a known key set; reach for Dynamic only when names are genuinely data-driven. Descriptors are hand-written or derived from case-class metadata.
code_sketch:
import scala.collection.mutable
import scala.language.dynamics

class Order extends Dynamic {
  private val props = mutable.Map.empty[String, Any]
  def selectDynamic(name: String): Option[Any] = props.get(name)
  def updateDynamic(name: String)(value: Any): Unit = props(name) = value
  def propertyNames: Set[String] = props.keySet          // discoverability
}

val o = new Order
o.colour = "red"            // o.updateDynamic("colour")("red")
o.id                        // o.selectDynamic("id") -> Option[Any]
pitfalls: Dynamic selection defeats the compiler: a typo compiles and becomes a runtime lookup (returning Option keeps absence visible; returning a plain value hides it), and IDE refactors no longer find usages.

Defining a Dynamic subclass requires the dynamics language feature (import scala.language.dynamics or -language:dynamics); the compiler rejects it otherwise, and the feature is off by default precisely because it weakens static checking.

The backing map must be guarded if the object crosses threads (scala.collection.mutable.Map has no synchronization), and updateDynamic needs a mutable map - an immutable one silently costs you the write path.
